title: Al-Gharra: The Prophet’s Expeditions
intro: In 1447 AH (2025 CE), Fawwaz ibn Jurays al-Dawsari composed Al-Gharra to help readers remember the expeditions Muhammad joined and those he entrusted to others. The route runs from Waddan through Badr, Uhud and Hudaybiya to Mecca and Tabuk, ending with the appointment of Usama. A watering place or a standard-bearer’s name can stand for a whole episode, and the poet sometimes preserves rival dates or claims of precedence.

translation: Praise to God who revealed himself
in justice and generosity, then bestowed blessings
1.sharh: The opening names justice and the doing of good as ways God makes himself known. The sentence waits for the next verse to name the recipient of blessing.

translation: on the Prophet of Quraysh, our guide,
who led us to victory and striving.
2.sharh: “Us” includes the later poet among the followers of the Meccan prophet. The idea of being led prepares for the many journeys about to be named.

translation: Take this short poem about the expeditions.
It lights lamps of instruction for the night traveller.
3.sharh: The poem is offered like something a traveller can carry. Recalled events become separate lamps along a dark road.

translation: In his second year he went to Waddan
and returned without meeting hostility there.
4.sharh: The years are counted from the migration to Medina. An expedition has a name and a place in this history even when no fighting took place.

translation: At Rabigh, Ubayda raised
the first banner of guidance, seeking God’s reward.
5.sharh: The standard marks command of a detachment. Its claim to be the first will be qualified two lines later.

translation: Among the archers Sa'd was first
to support the faith, and so became an example.
6.sharh: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas is remembered in the accounts of Ubayda’s expedition as the first to loose an arrow for Islam. The distinction is different from carrying the earliest banner.

translation: Another account gives the first victorious standard
to God’s Lion on the seashore.
7.sharh: Two early expeditions were close enough in time for their order to be disputed. God’s Lion is Muhammad’s uncle Hamza.

translation: Towards Buwat, in Rabi' al-Awwal,
the best of messengers led God’s company.
8.sharh: The place and the lunar month come before the traveller’s identity. The sources remember the journey even though no engagement followed.

translation: Afterwards at al-Ushayra he made peace
with the sons of Mudlij and the sons of Damra.
9.sharh: The journey brings a treaty into the sequence. The two tribal names place the agreement among communities along the route.

translation: The Chosen One sent to al-Kharrar
Sa'd and his band, without the Helpers.
10.sharh: Sa'd now commands a party of his own. Excluding the Helpers distinguishes Muhammad’s Meccan emigrant followers from their Medinan hosts.

translation: Then came Safwan, the first Badr.
Kurz proved rash in his raid.
11.sharh: The pursuit reached the vicinity of Badr, hence “first Badr”. The famous battle of that name still lies ahead.

translation: The Prophet sent Abd Allah
to Nakhla, and he was intent upon his task.
12.sharh: Nakhla identifies Abd Allah as Ibn Jahsh. The sequel will make the incident a question about sacred time.

translation: He faced the sacred month, saying, “Here you are.”
Then came the verse, “They ask you.”
13.sharh: The words cue Qur’an 2.217, a response to the question of fighting in a sacred month. The opening alone is enough to call up the passage.

translation: Then the Almighty brought the day of distinction
between the hosts of unbelief and faith.
14.sharh: Qur’an 8.41 calls the day the two hosts met “the day of distinction”. It is this title, rather than the place name, that announces the main battle of Badr.

translation: On a Monday in the month of fasting,
after eight nights he set out with his people.
15.sharh: The “month of fasting” locates the departure in Ramadan. The elapsed nights refer to setting out, before the date later given for the battle.

translation: He sought a caravan of Quraysh, but it escaped.
God ordained a battle that flared up instead.
16.sharh: The expected encounter was with a trading caravan. Its escape changes the story into one about an armed meeting the poet understands as divinely ordained.

translation: He wanted the support of the Helpers.
Sa'd rose and pledged it in a speech.
17.sharh: The speaker is Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, speaking for Medinan allies. Earlier mentions of Sa'd concerned a different companion.

translation: Once ten days and seven had gone,
they fought, and my Lord’s messengers were sent down.
18.sharh: Ten plus seven fixes the battle on the seventeenth of Ramadan. The messengers in the second half are angels, recalling the aid promised in Qur’an 8.9.

translation: They struck down seventy in the fighting
and took as many prisoners in bonds.
19.sharh: The familiar account gives the same total for those killed and those captured. That symmetry makes the figures easier to remember.

translation: Remember Umayr and his killing of Asma,
and Salim, who answered the call.
20.sharh: Two disputed reports in the campaign literature concern the deaths of Asma bint Marwan and Abu Afak. The lines reflect their place in that literature, where their chains of transmission are weak.

translation: Then at al-Kudr he drew a keen sword
against Sulaym and came safely home.
21.sharh: Drawing a sword stands for setting out. Sulaym, the tribal name, echoes salim, the word for coming home safe.

translation: Then came al-Sawiq, when Sakhr raided.
Seeing the Messenger he said, “Flee.”
22.sharh: Al-Sawiq takes its name from a meal of ground grain that the retreating party reportedly discarded. The poet gives their withdrawal the immediacy of speech.

translation: He prolonged his stay in the month of Safar,
keeping watch for God in the midst of Dhu Amarr.
23.sharh: The memorable part of this expedition is time spent away. The poet places it in Safar, one of the dates in the campaign tradition.

translation: Later they stayed at Buhran
two months without meeting spears there.
24.sharh: A second period of waiting follows the first. Spears stand for the fighting that never materialised.

translation: He tells of Qaynuqa' breaking their covenants
and calls malice part of Jewish nature.
25.sharh: The episode concerns Banu Qaynuqa', one Jewish community in Medina. The second half extends the poet’s accusation to Jews as a people, a derogatory generalisation for which the episode provides no basis.

translation: And Zayd, when my Lord’s Messenger entrusted him
with reaching their caravan at al-Qarada.
26.sharh: Zayd ibn Haritha was entrusted with the expedition known by the watering place al-Qarada. The caravan motif recalls how much of the early narrative follows trade routes.

translation: Remember the march at Uhud in Shawwal,
then the muster for Hamra al-Asad.
27.sharh: The battle of Uhud and the march to Hamra al-Asad belong together here. The second followed the first while its effects were still being felt.

translation: The archers disobeyed for the spoils.
It was a lesson to those who disobey the law.
28.sharh: The poet follows the Qur’anic recollection of divided intentions at Uhud. The wish for spoils gives an ethical meaning to what happened.

translation: After it came al-Raji', then the well
of Ma'una. Treachery showed itself in both.
29.sharh: The two names recall men from Medina killed after going out at others’ invitation. The poetic break keeps the reader waiting for the name of the well.

translation: Then the designs of Banu al-Nadir came to light.
The Chosen One drove them out, as The Gathering recounts.
30.sharh: The campaign accounts explain the break with this Medinan community through an alleged plot. Qur’an 59 opens with the expulsion to which the poet refers.

translation: Dhat al-Riqa' was dated to the fourth year.
There the prayer in danger was duly instituted.
31.sharh: The poet places Dhat al-Riqa' in year four. Its date is disputed, but reports regularly connect it with a way of praying in a time of danger.

translation: Then he went to Badr for the appointed meeting.
Count Dumat al-Jandal after it.
32.sharh: This is Badr again, now named for a rendezvous arranged after Uhud. The instruction to count keeps the later northern journey in sequence.

translation: Ibn Unays felled horsemen
at Nakhla, seeking to kill the man he calls a devil.
33.sharh: The campaign tradition identifies the man as Khalid ibn Sufyan. “Devil” gives the poet’s hostile estimate of a human opponent.

translation: The confederates assembled at the trench,
and Qurayza did not keep the pact.
34.sharh: “Confederates” denotes the coalition that besieged Medina. The campaign narrative places the breach it attributes to Banu Qurayza during that siege.

translation: God sent his hosts against them.
In overcoming the besieging host he kept his promise.
35.sharh: Qur’an 33.9 recalls a wind and forces the believers could not see. The poet treats the lifting of the siege as the fulfilment of a promise.

translation: Ibn Mu'adh gave judgement,
and the mighty King’s throne shook.
36.sharh: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh arbitrated in the case of Qurayza. The saying about the throne belongs to his death soon afterwards.

translation: Remember Banu Lihyan and Dhu Qarad.
The man of Fazara raided the town’s grazing herd.
37.sharh: Two expeditions share the line. It is the second, Dhu Qarad, that concerns Medina’s grazing animals and a raider from Fazara.

translation: Then came al-Muraysi', dated by some
to year four, when our mother was cleared.
38.sharh: The campaign is named for its watering place. “Our mother” is Aisha, whom Muslim tradition identifies as the subject of the vindication in Qur’an 24.

translation: Zayd set out and surprised Judham.
Afterwards he nearly met his death.
39.sharh: The poem moves straight from Judham to a later reverse associated with Fazara. The rhyme word is an old name for death.

translation: Remember Kurz’s march, and Ibn Awf’s
to Dumat al-Jandal without fear.
40.sharh: Kurz and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf commanded separate expeditions. Dumat al-Jandal is the destination of the second.

translation: And al-Yusayr’s death short of Khaybar,
and Ibn Uthal, whose story al-Maqburi reported.
41.sharh: The first name belongs to a fatal encounter near Khaybar. The second recalls Thumama, brought to Medina as a captive, who subsequently embraced Islam.

translation: And Amir, when his company ran out of supplies
and God brought forth a great fish from the sea for them.
42.sharh: Amir is Abu Ubayda. Jabir’s account describes the hungry company finding a great sea creature washed ashore and living on it.

translation: Then he concluded peace with Quraysh.
My Lord called it a victory in the Book.
43.sharh: The treaty at Hudaybiya takes the narrative from campaigning to negotiation. The opening of Qur’an 48 gives the result its unexpected name, a victory.

translation: Early in year seven came Khaybar’s fall.
Ja'far’s arrival coincided with the victory.
44.sharh: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib returned with fellow emigrants from Abyssinia. The convergence makes the date a family reunion as well as a public event.

translation: Ghalib’s riders went to Murra,
and Ibn Abi Hadrad towards al-Ghaba.
45.sharh: Two compact assignments pair a commander with a destination. One is a tribe, the other a place whose name means woodland.

translation: Madyan yielded to victorious Zayd.
Ghalib’s riders set out for al-Kudayd.
46.sharh: “Victorious” in the first half has the same Arabic form as the commander’s name Ghalib in the second. The wordplay fastens two separate journeys together.

translation: Amr joined battle at Dhat al-Salasil,
and Ibn Abi Hadrad was in the valley of Idam.
47.sharh: Amr is Ibn al-As. A verb of movement is left for the listener to supply in the second half, where a man and a valley suffice.

translation: At Mu'ta, Zayd led the company,
then Ja'far, then Ibn Rawaha followed.
48.sharh: The names follow the order in which the three commanders bore the standard at Mu'ta. Quick successive “thens” register the passing of responsibility.

translation: Then came the opening, and falsehood vanished
in Mecca, and the tribes submitted.
49.sharh: The “opening” is the Muslim entry into Mecca. Language recalling Qur’an 17.81 presents it as a religious turning point as well as a change in power.

translation: Remember Hunayn, and their delight in their numbers.
“Our army will never lose for want of men.”
50.sharh: Qur’an 9.25 recalls the believers’ pleasure in their numbers at Hunayn. The second half voices the confidence the experience would call into question.

translation: God made the Prophet stand firm, and he prevailed.
Then he urged those present on to Ta'if.
51.sharh: The narrative answers confidence in numbers with steadfastness given by God. Ta'if is the next destination.

translation: In the ninth year he went to Tabuk,
and the standing of kings was shaken.
52.sharh: The poem gives the march to Tabuk a political effect on regional rulers. No battle with a Byzantine army took place there.

translation: Yuhanna made a treaty with them for tribute,
and Khalid put Duma’s ruler in bonds.
53.sharh: Yuhanna ruled Ayla. The ruler of Duma taken by Khalid was Ukaydir, a different man in a different episode.

translation: Uyayna came upon Banu al-Anbar in the morning.
Ibn Mujazziz returned without exacting vengeance.
54.sharh: Uyayna’s episode concerns Banu al-Anbar. Alqama ibn Mujazziz led a separate coastal expedition and returned without an engagement.

translation: Ali went south and followed,
on returning for pilgrimage, the Chosen One’s example.
55.sharh: South means Yemen. On joining Muhammad for the Farewell Pilgrimage, Ali declared the same intention for the pilgrimage rites as the Prophet had.

translation: The Chosen One appointed, for Syria,
Usama, who had the honour of coming last.
56.sharh: Usama ibn Zayd received his command near the end of Muhammad’s life. The army departed after his death, so the appointment closes this sequence.

translation: Praise to him who revealed himself and is exalted.
My Lord, bless the best of humankind,
57.sharh: The verb about God’s self-disclosure brings back the opening line. The blessing that follows carries over into the last verse.

translation: his family and companions, and whoever followed
their footsteps and drew on the radiance of truth.
58.sharh: Those who follow inherit footsteps and light. The image answers the lamps lit for the night traveller near the beginning.

2.1.3.head: القُرَشِيّ
2.1.3.meaning: Qurashi, a member of Quraysh, Muhammad’s Meccan tribe.

3.1.4.head: المَغازي
3.1.4.meaning: Maghazi, accounts of Muhammad’s expeditions and, by extension, detachments he sent.

4.1.5.head: وَدّان
4.1.5.meaning: Waddan, a place between Mecca and Medina, associated with the expedition also named al-Abwa.

5.1.2.head: رابِغ
5.1.2.meaning: Rabigh, a district on the coastal route through the Hijaz.

5.1.3.head: عُبَيدَة
5.1.3.meaning: Ubayda ibn al-Harith, an early Meccan emigrant.

5.2.4.head: اِحتَسَبَ
5.2.4.meaning: Sought God’s reward for what he did.

5.2.2.head: رايَة
5.2.2.meaning: A standard. The booklet has the plural, “standards”.

6.1.2.head: سَعد
6.1.2.meaning: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, the emigrant singled out as an archer in this expedition.

7.1.4.head: رايَة
7.1.4.meaning: A battle standard. The written version again uses the plural.

7.2.2-3.head: لَيث اللَّه
7.2.2-3.meaning: “God’s Lion”, a name for the Prophet’s uncle Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib.

7.2.5-6.head: سيف البَحر
7.2.5-6.meaning: “The edge of the sea”, the seashore.

8.1.2.head: بُواط
8.1.2.meaning: Buwat, a place near Mount Radwa in the Hijaz.

9.1.4.head: العُشَيرَة
9.1.4.meaning: Al-Ushayra, a place in the Yanbu area.

9.2.3-4.head: بَنو ضَمرَة
9.2.3-4.meaning: Banu Damra, a branch of Kinana that made treaties with the Medinans. The booklet says “the sons of Damra”. The sung word may be the singular “son”.

10.1.3.head: الخَرّار
10.1.3.meaning: Al-Kharrar, the site of Sa'd’s expedition. The singing sounds like al-Jarrar.

10.2.4.head: الأَنصار
10.2.4.meaning: Ansar, the Medinan Muslims who sheltered the emigrants.

11.1.2.head: سَفوان
11.1.2.meaning: Safwan, a valley near Badr reached on this expedition.

11.2.2.head: كُرز
11.2.2.meaning: Kurz ibn Jabir, a man of Fihr who later became Muslim and commanded a separate expedition.

12.1.3-4.head: عَبد اللَّه
12.1.3-4.meaning: Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, commander of the Nakhla expedition.

12.2.1.head: نَخلَة
12.2.1.meaning: Nakhla, a place between Mecca and Ta'if.

13.1.2-3.head: الشَّهر الحَرام
13.1.2-3.meaning: “The sacred month”, here Rajab, one of four traditionally protected months.

14.1.4.head: الفُرقان
14.1.4.meaning: Furqan, a distinction or criterion, applied to Badr in Qur’an 8.41.

17.1.4-5.head: أَهل النُّصرَة
17.1.4-5.meaning: “The people of aid”, Muhammad’s Medinan supporters.

17.2.2.head: سَعد
17.2.2.meaning: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, a leader of the Aws in Medina.

19.1.4.head: الوَغى
19.1.4.meaning: The din of combat, then battle itself.

20.1.2.head: عُمَير
20.1.2.meaning: Umayr ibn Adi, named in the disputed report concerning Asma.

20.1.4.head: العَصماء
20.1.4.meaning: Asma bint Marwan, named in a report of her death whose chain is unreliable.

20.2.1.head: سالِم
20.2.1.meaning: Salim ibn Umayr, named in the report about Abu Afak.

21.1.2.head: الكُدر
21.1.2.meaning: Al-Kudr, a watering place associated with Banu Sulaym.

22.1.2.head: السَّويق
22.1.2.meaning: Sawiq, ground roasted grain, here the name of an expedition.

22.1.5.head: صَخر
22.1.5.meaning: Sakhr ibn Harb, better known as Abu Sufyan.

23.2.4-5.head: ذو أَمَر
23.2.4-5.meaning: Dhu Amarr, a place in Najd which gives the Ghatafan expedition one of its names.

24.1.5.head: بُحران
24.1.5.meaning: Buhran, a place in the Hijaz visited in the third year after the migration.

25.1.2.head: قَينُقاع
25.1.2.meaning: Qaynuqa', a Jewish community in Medina.

25.2.3.head: جِبِلَّة
25.2.3.meaning: An innate disposition. The poet uses the word here in a derogatory generalisation about Jews.

26.1.1.head: زَيد
26.1.1.meaning: Zayd ibn Haritha, Muhammad’s freedman and a commander of several detachments.

26.2.5.head: القَرَدَة
26.2.5.meaning: Al-Qarada, a watering place in Najd on the caravan’s route.

27.1.5.head: أُحُد
27.1.5.meaning: Uhud, the mountain just north of Medina that gave the battle its name.

27.2.4-5.head: حَمراء الأَسَد
27.2.4-5.meaning: Hamra al-Asad, a place south of Medina reached after Uhud.

28.2.4.head: الشِّرعَة
28.2.4.meaning: The divinely appointed way or law.

29.1.2.head: الرَّجيع
29.1.2.meaning: Al-Raji', a watering place in Hudhayl territory associated with the deaths of several companions.

29.2.1.head: مَعونَة
29.2.1.meaning: Ma'una, a well in Najd where a group of Qur’an reciters was killed.

30.1.2-3.head: بَنو النَّضير
30.1.2-3.meaning: Banu al-Nadir, a Jewish community living near Medina.

30.2.5.head: الحَشر
30.2.5.meaning: Al-Hashr, “The Gathering”, chapter 59 of the Qur’an.

31.1.3-4.head: ذات الرِّقاع
31.1.3-4.meaning: Dhat al-Riqa', an expedition of disputed date.

31.2.2-3.head: صَلاة الخَوف
31.2.2-3.meaning: “Prayer in danger”, a form of prayer discussed in Qur’an 4.102.

32.1.4-5.head: بَدر المَوعِد
32.1.4-5.meaning: Badr al-Maw'id, the expedition to the rendezvous agreed after Uhud.

32.2.1-2.head: دومَة الجَندَل
32.2.1-2.meaning: Dumat al-Jandal, an oasis town in northern Arabia.

33.1.1-2.head: اِبن أُنَيس
33.1.1-2.meaning: Ibn Unays, Abd Allah of Juhayna, the companion named in the Nakhla account.

33.1.3.head: جَندَلَ
33.1.3.meaning: Felled or cast to the ground.

34.1.2.head: الأَحزاب
34.1.2.meaning: The Confederates, the coalition that besieged Medina.

34.2.3.head: قُرَيظَة
34.2.3.meaning: Qurayza, a Jewish community in Medina.

36.1.1-2.head: اِبن مُعاذ
36.1.1-2.meaning: Ibn Mu'adh, Sa'd, whose judgement was sought in the Qurayza affair.

37.1.5-6.head: ذو قَرَد
37.1.5-6.meaning: Dhu Qarad, a watering place associated with the raid also known as al-Ghaba.

37.2.4.head: سَرح
37.2.4.meaning: A herd turned out to graze.

38.1.2.head: المُرَيسيع
38.1.2.meaning: Al-Muraysi', a watering place of Banu al-Mustaliq.

38.2.4.head: أُمّنا
38.2.4.meaning: “Our mother”, Aisha, one of Muhammad’s wives, known as the Mothers of the Believers.

39.1.5.head: جُذام
39.1.5.meaning: Judham, an Arab tribe in the northern Hijaz and southern Syria.

40.1.4-5.head: اِبن عَوف
40.1.4-5.meaning: Ibn Awf, Abd al-Rahman, one of the early emigrants.

41.1.2.head: اليُسَير
41.1.2.meaning: Al-Yusayr, also named Usayr ibn Rizam, a man from Khaybar.

41.2.1-2.head: اِبن أُثال
41.2.1-2.meaning: Ibn Uthal, Thumama, a leader of Banu Hanifa in Yamama.

41.2.5.head: المَقبُري
41.2.5.meaning: Al-Maqburi, Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id, who transmitted Abu Hurayra’s account of Thumama.

42.1.1.head: عامِر
42.1.1.meaning: Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah, known as Abu Ubayda.

43.2.5.head: فَتح
43.2.5.meaning: An opening or victory, here the peace made at Hudaybiya.

44.1.5.head: خَيبَر
44.1.5.meaning: Khaybar, a fortified oasis north of Medina.

44.2.4.head: جَعفَر
44.2.4.meaning: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad’s cousin and Ali’s brother.

45.1.3.head: غالِب
45.1.3.meaning: Ghalib ibn Abd Allah al-Laythi, a commander mentioned in several expedition accounts.

45.2.1-3.head: اِبن أَبي حَدرَد
45.2.1-3.meaning: Ibn Abi Hadrad, Abd Allah of Aslam, a companion.

46.1.1.head: مَديَن
46.1.1.meaning: Madyan, the region of Midian in north-western Arabia.

46.2.2.head: الكُدَيد
46.2.2.meaning: Al-Kudayd, a place near Qudayd on the Hejazi route.

47.1.1.head: عَمرٌو
47.1.1.meaning: Amr ibn al-As, commander at Dhat al-Salasil.

47.1.3-4.head: ذات السَّلاسِل
47.1.3-4.meaning: Dhat al-Salasil, the place that gave Amr’s expedition its name.

47.2.6.head: إِضَم
47.2.6.meaning: Idam, a valley in the Hijaz.

48.1.1.head: مُؤتَة
48.1.1.meaning: Mu'ta, a settlement in what is now Jordan.

48.2.2-3.head: اِبن رَواحَة
48.2.2-3.meaning: Ibn Rawaha, Abd Allah, a Medinan poet and one of the commanders at Mu'ta.

50.1.2.head: حُنَين
50.1.2.meaning: Hunayn, a valley between Mecca and Ta'if.

52.1.5.head: تَبوك
52.1.5.meaning: Tabuk, an oasis in north-western Arabia reached in year nine.

53.1.1.head: يُحَنَّة
53.1.1.meaning: Yuhanna ibn Ru'ba, ruler of Ayla on the Gulf of Aqaba.

53.1.3.head: الجِزيَة
53.1.3.meaning: Jizya, a payment under treaty, here associated with Ayla.

53.2.1.head: خالِد
53.2.1.meaning: Khalid ibn al-Walid, who led the expedition to Ukaydir of Duma.

54.1.1.head: عُيَينَة
54.1.1.meaning: Uyayna ibn Hisn, a leader of Fazara.

54.2.1-2.head: اِبن مُجَزِّز
54.2.1-2.meaning: Ibn Mujazziz, Alqama of Mudlij. The reciter appears to end the name with r.

55.1.2.head: عَلِيّ
55.1.2.meaning: Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad’s cousin and Fatima’s husband.

56.2.1.head: أُسامَة
56.2.1.meaning: Usama ibn Zayd ibn Haritha, appointed shortly before Muhammad’s death.
